name: Chloe Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the health and social care correspondent for Westmoor Radio, which is the local station and news website of a public broadcaster. A normal day starts with the 7am editorial call, then I'm usually out at the hospital, a care home or a GP surgery recording interviews. I cut a two-minute radio piece for the drive-time bulletin and write a longer version for the website. The best part is when a family trusts me with something they've never told anyone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The budget. Our funding's been frozen for three years, so every time someone leaves, the post sits empty for months. I'm twenty-seven and I'm already the person juniors come to with questions. My partner Tom is a nurse on the stroke ward at Westmoor General, so we both come home talking about the same hospital from opposite sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the real problem, which is that public news is being starved. I'd post something like that and probably get a few hundred angry replies. AI being hype doesn't fix a frozen budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my own job is fairly safe, because health reporting needs someone who'll sit in a waiting room for three hours. But the team around me keeps shrinking anyway. If AI is a damp squib, the cuts just carry on under a different excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job I do, and I'd keep using the transcription tool I already use now and then for long interviews. I'd keep our savings ticking along at about £200 a month, which gets us to roughly three months. And I'd stay active in the union branch, because the next funding round is what decides whether my job survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a low hum of worry. It's the background noise I already live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the funding freeze. Does that worry you more than AI in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. AI-as-hype is the most likely future in my head, and in that one the risk is a politician deciding public radio is a luxury. That's happened to two neighbouring stations already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one routine task you'd actually be glad to hand over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Typing up interviews. Last week I had a ninety-minute conversation with a care home manager and spent most of an evening transcribing it. If a tool can do that reliably, I'd hand it over gladly and spend the time on the phone instead.

say: AI being hype doesn't fix the **frozen budget** starving public news.
The real fight is the **next funding round**, not software.
think: Health reporting needs someone who'll **sit in a waiting room** for hours, so my job feels fairly safe.
The team keeps **shrinking anyway**, under whatever excuse is handy.
do: Keep using the **transcription tool** now and then for long interviews.
Save about **£200 a month**, reaching roughly three months.
Stay active in the **union branch** ahead of the funding round.
feel: Mostly fine, with a **low hum** of worry she already lives with.
S0.quote: Health reporting needs someone who'll sit in a waiting room for three hours.
fieldNote: Her worry in the calm picture is **political funding**, not AI.
Already uses AI **for transcription only**, and sees it as a time saver.
Two **neighbouring stations** have already closed, which shapes her caution.

steps.text: Keep reporting from hospitals, care homes and surgeries as now
Put about £200 a month into joint savings with Tom
Campaign through the union branch ahead of the next funding round

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear rules on AI in public news: humans make the editorial calls, and any AI use is declared to listeners. I'd say it at work and online. And I'd say public broadcasters should be the ones setting the standard, not copying the tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of what we do would go to software fast. The bulletin scripts, the website rewrites, checking press releases from the health trust: that's writing and checking, which is on your list. I'd probably keep a job, but it might be one where I'm producing for a machine instead of reporting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly, through the training the broadcaster would surely offer, because by then other stations would have shown it works. I'd push the union to get a deal that no posts are cut without a year's notice. And I'd lift savings to £300 a month, which means fewer dinners out and no new phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into anxious. Like waiting for a team meeting you know has bad news in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools properly now. Why now and not before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by then it's proven. I don't jump at every shiny thing, but once colleagues at bigger stations are using it every day and it doesn't make mistakes with names and numbers, I'd be silly not to learn it. Refusing would just make me easier to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our bulletin producer, Graham, who's been there twenty years. He's brilliant, but his whole job is turning copy into tight 30-second reads, and that's exactly what the software would be good at. I'd worry about him before I'd worry about me.

say: Humans should make the **editorial calls**, and AI use should be declared.
Public broadcasters should **set the standard**, not copy the tech firms.
think: Bulletin scripts and **website rewrites** would go to software fast.
I might end up **producing for a machine** instead of reporting.
do: Learn the AI tools through **broadcaster training** once they're proven elsewhere.
Push the union for **a year's notice** before any post is cut.
Lift savings to **£300 a month** by eating out less.
feel: **Anxious**, like waiting for a meeting she knows holds bad news.
S1.quote: I'd probably keep a job, but it might be one where I'm producing for a machine instead of reporting.
fieldNote: Steady about technology: she'll adopt once **colleagues prove it**.
Worries first about **Graham (bulletin producer)**, whose work is most automatable.
Sees refusing tools as making her **easier to cut**.

steps.text: Take the broadcaster's AI training once other stations prove it works
Push the union branch for a year's notice before any post is cut
Cut dinners out and skip a new phone to save £300 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have failed everyone by letting this happen with no plan. I'd be shouting for an emergency fund for public-interest journalism and for anyone thrown out of work. That's the post I'd write, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2028 a broadcaster could run a local news service with a handful of editors and the AI. My whole job is thinking work: interviewing, writing, deciding what matters. The robots coming later doesn't help me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by making sure Tom and I could live on his nurse's pay, which means cutting about £400 a month. I'd look hard at moving into health communications at the hospital trust while there are still posts. And I'd join every union and campaign push for a public jobs guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the ground I trained on for six years has gone soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your job is truly hands-on, the part robots would need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost none, really. I drive to places and hold a microphone, but a camera on a stand could do that. The bit that matters is knowing which question to ask a grieving daughter, and that's thinking work, so it's on the 2028 date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom actually decide in that first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit down and cut the extras: the car share upgrade, the streaming bills, the weekend away we'd booked. We'd agree that Tom's job is the anchor for now. And I'd apply for the comms job at the trust that same month, even if it felt like giving up.

say: Governments have **failed everyone** by letting this happen with no plan.
We need an **emergency fund** for public-interest journalism and displaced workers.
think: A broadcaster could run local news with **a handful of editors** and AI by 2028.
My work is **thinking work**, so the robot delay doesn't help me.
do: Cut about **£400 a month** so the household lives on Tom's nurse pay.
Apply for **health communications** at the hospital trust.
Join union and campaign pushes for a **jobs guarantee**.
feel: **Frightened**, like the ground she trained on has gone soft.
S2.quote: The bit that matters is knowing which question to ask a grieving daughter, and that's thinking work, so it's on the 2028 date.
fieldNote: She sees her **hands-on share** as almost nil, so AGI hits her on the stated date.
Partner Tom's **nursing job** becomes the household anchor.
Would apply for comms work while feeling it is **giving up**.

steps.text: Cut about £400 a month so the household runs on Tom's pay
Apply for a health communications post at the hospital trust
Campaign with the union for a public jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this decently if politicians start now. Fund retraining, protect public media, tax the companies. That's what I'd say in the newsroom and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd still lose the reporting job around 2031. But five years is enough to finish a qualification and land somewhere on purpose, not in a panic. That's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time master's in health policy in year one, paid partly from savings, about £3,000 a year. I'd keep reporting and use the AI tools more as they settle in. And I'd keep savings growing to five months, so we could cover a gap between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Like knowing the exam date in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years versus two: what's the biggest thing the extra time changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get to choose. With two years I'd grab whatever job was open. With five years I can steer toward health policy, where I know the people, and arrive with a qualification instead of a begging email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to health. Why that and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Tom's on the stroke ward and I've spent five years in care homes, so health is the world I know. And the people in it will still need someone who can explain hard things plainly to the public. I'd rather be that person than chase something I don't care about.

say: Five years is enough to do this **decently** if politicians start now.
Fund **retraining**, protect public media and tax the AI companies.
think: Five years lets me land somewhere **on purpose**, not in panic.
do: Start a part-time **health policy master's**, about £3,000 a year.
Use the **AI tools** more as they settle in.
Grow savings to **five months** to cover a gap between jobs.
feel: **Anxious but planned**, like knowing an exam date in advance.
S3.quote: With five years I can steer toward health policy and arrive with a qualification instead of a begging email.
fieldNote: The extra time turns a scramble into a **chosen move** toward health policy.
Draws on partner Tom's **ward** and her own beat for the next career.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in health policy at about £3,000 a year
Use the station's AI tools more as they settle in
Build joint savings up to five months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to protect what matters, so there's no excuse. Public news, care workers, nurses: these should be protected by policy now. That's my public line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-seven when it hits. I think I'd have a good run in reporting still, then move into health policy or communications properly. Tom's job is hands-on and should be safe until the robots, so the household feels steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting and take on the AI tools as they become normal at the station. I'd start the health policy course in year three or four rather than now. And I'd vote and campaign for whoever promises public money for local news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can carry. It's more like weather on the horizon than a storm overhead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything about whether you stay in news at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd stay in news for most of the decade. It's what I'm good at, and ten years is long enough for the station to change shape a few times. I'd just make sure I'm not the last one out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund public news properly and attach rules to AI used in it. And start real retraining money now, so people like Graham at the station aren't left at sixty with nothing.

say: Ten years is plenty, so there's **no excuse** not to protect public news.
Care workers and nurses should be **protected by policy** now.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when it hits, with a good run in reporting first.
Tom's **hands-on job** keeps the household steadier until the robots.
do: Keep reporting and adopt AI tools as they become **normal** at the station.
Start a **health policy course** in year three or four.
Vote and campaign for **public money** for local news.
feel: **Uneasy** but bearable, like weather on the horizon.
S4.quote: I'd be thirty-seven when it hits, and I think I'd have a good run in reporting still.
fieldNote: The decade makes her **unhurried**: she would delay retraining.
The **nurse partner's** hands-on job steadies the household view.
Still thinks of colleague **Graham** near sixty.

steps.text: Keep reporting the health beat at Westmoor Radio
Use the station's AI tools as they become standard
Campaign for public funding of local news before elections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to land anywhere on purpose. What would help is retraining money that starts before the job goes, and a guarantee that public news keeps real reporters on the ground.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we report on. If the reporters go, nobody tells the story of the care home with one carer for twenty residents. That's what I'd actually lose sleep over.

headlineQuote: If the reporters go, nobody tells the story of the care home with one carer for twenty residents.
portrait: A **27-year-old** health correspondent at a public broadcaster's local radio station.
Uses AI for **transcription** and adopts more once colleagues prove it works.
Blames **underfunding** and government more than technology, and backs unions and public money.
Moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at AGI in two years, settling to uneasy with ten.
Partner Tom's **nursing job** is the household anchor, and she'd move toward health policy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which gives no time to land in a new career on purpose.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining money** that starts before jobs go.
A guarantee that public news keeps **real reporters**.
